'''''Monstera acuminata''''', or '''shingle plant''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Araceae]] which is widespread from Mexico to Central America.<ref name=POWO/> It is abundant in central [[Petén Department|Petén]] and extends north to [[San Luis Potosí]], making it the northernmost species of ''[[Monstera]].''<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://e-monocot.org/taxon/urn:kew.org:wcs:taxon:129568|title=''Monstera acuminata'' K.Koch|website=e-monocot.org|access-date=2016-10-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161029044736/http://e-monocot.org/taxon/urn:kew.org:wcs:taxon:129568|archive-date=2016-10-29}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Monstera acuminata'' germinates in the ground and grows horizontally as a low prostrate herb.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=López-Portillo|first1=J.|last2=Ewers|first2=F. W.|last3=Angeles|first3=G.|last4=Fisher|first4=J. B.|date=2000-02-01|title=Hydraulic architecture of Monstera acuminata: evolutionary consequences of the hemiepiphytic growth form|journal=New Phytologist|language=en|volume=145|issue=2|pages=289–299|doi=10.1046/j.1469-8137.2000.00578.x|issn=1469-8137|doi-access=free}}</ref> The juvenile plant is much smaller and heart-shaped with thick, roundish, waxy leaves which grow in two ranks and overlap each other with the stem elliptic in cross section and internodes 1–5 cm long and asymmetric leaves.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

When it encounters a tree trunk, it uses its ageotropic anchoring roots to grow vertically.<ref name=":2" /> The adult plant appears similar to that of ''[[Monstera deliciosa]]'' and these leaves are developed when the plant reaches 15 feet and is an example of [[Sexual dimorphism|dimorphism]]. The leaves are smooth or papillose stem 2–3.5 cm thick with internodes 6–11 cm long.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LfU5AQAAIAAJ&dq=Monstera+acuminata&pg=PA1028|title=Cyclopedia of American Horticulture: Comprising Suggestions for Cultivation of Horticultural Plants, Descriptions of the Species of Fruits, Vegetables, Flowers and Ornamental Plants Sold in the United States and Canada, Together with Geographical and Biographical Sketches, and a Synopsis of the Vegetable Kingdom|last=Miller|first=Wilhelm|date=1906-01-01|publisher=Doubleday, Page|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> After it grows upwards, the base of the stem of the [[hemiepiphyte]] dies and rots, thereby losing its connection to the soil.<ref name=":2" />
